content: Three patients experienced grade 3 adverse events, and two patients experienced grade 4 adverse events. It is recommended to perform a complete blood count with differential before initiating linezolid treatment, then every two weeks for the first two months, and subsequently every four weeks during treatment. This monitoring strategy is essential for the early detection of adverse events, such as reductions in hemoglobin, platelet, or neutrophil counts. Temporary discontinuation of linezolid may be necessary in cases of worsening cytopenias to allow for the evaluation of other potential causes. Anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia are typically reversible upon cessation of linezolid. However, in cases of severe cytopenias, permanent discontinuation of linezolid may be required. If linezolid is a critical component of the treatment regimen, it may be restarted at a lower dose. Monitoring for other toxicities associated with linezolid, such as peripheral neuropathy and optic neuritis, is also crucial. Reflex testing at baseline or regular pinprick testing can be employed to monitor for these toxicities. Visual acuity should be assessed in children at baseline and throughout treatment using symbol charts or tumbling E charts. For infants and toddlers, visual tracking of objects like a finger or small toy can be used. Neuropsychiatric side effects, including hallucinations, should be closely monitored in children receiving medications known to cause such effects, such as delamanid and cycloserine. Any neuropsychiatric events should be reported to the national pharmacovigilance system. Hypothyroidism is a common adverse effect of ethionamide, prothionamide, and para-aminosalicylic acid, with an increased risk when para-aminosalicylic acid is combined with ethionamide or prothionamide. Symptoms of hypothyroidism are often nonspecific and challenging to assess in young children. Hypothyroidism can negatively impact neurodevelopment in young children. Regular thyroid function tests every two months are recommended for all children on these medications until treatment is discontinued. Levothyroxine supplementation should be initiated if clinical or laboratory evidence of hypothyroidism is present. For hepatotoxicity monitoring, baseline measurements of ALT, with or without AST and bilirubin levels, are recommended. ALT should be repeated every four weeks for the first six months, every eight weeks thereafter, and as clinically indicated. Clinical indications for liver function testing include new-onset vomiting, abdominal pain or tenderness (especially in the right upper quadrant), and jaundice. If jaundice or elevated bilirubin and ALT levels are observed, or if ALT levels exceed three times the normal range with symptoms or five times the normal range without symptoms, all hepatotoxic medications should be immediately discontinued. Other causes of liver dysfunction, such as hepatitis A, B, or C, should be excluded. Hepatotoxic TB medications can be cautiously reintroduced one by one after normalization of liver enzymes, provided the treatment regimen is not failing. Alternative TB medications may be considered to replace hepatotoxic drugs. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes the importance of health education and counseling to improve treatment adherence in children and adolescents with TB. Adherence counseling and support for the child or adolescent and their family are critical for effective care, particularly in cases of multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB). Strong social support, family counseling, and close relationships with healthcare providers enhance care and treatment outcomes. Children and adolescents should be encouraged to resume normal activities, such as school and sports, once they are clinically stable and no longer infectious. Recommended adherence interventions include digital monitoring, material and psychological support, and staff education. Counseling tools and a family-centered approach to treatment and prevention of drug-resistant TB in children and adolescents have been developed by organizations like Médecins Sans Frontières. Post-TB health awareness has increased, highlighting the need to address the long-term consequences of TB beyond survival and treatment completion. Each child or adolescent on TB treatment should have a clearly defined treatment outcome at the end of therapy, but follow-up care may extend beyond treatment completion. Improved data on post-TB health will help quantify and monitor the burden of morbidity after treatment and guide evidence-based interventions to improve long-term outcomes. Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is the most debilitating form of TB in children, with high rates of neurological sequelae despite treatment. It disproportionately affects children under five years of age. Approximately 50% of children with TBM experience neurological sequelae, with more advanced disease stages at diagnosis associated with worse outcomes. Severe functional and neurocognitive disabilities are observed in 12–26% of children with TBM, requiring long-term care and support. Long-term outcomes for children surviving TBM into adulthood are poorly documented, and there is limited information on neurocognitive, functional, and behavioral impairments. Standardized tools for assessing neurodevelopmental and neurocognitive outcomes are available, and neuroimaging is generally not indicated due to poor correlation with developmental outcomes. Hydrocephalus occurs in 80% of children with advanced TBM, with 20% requiring ventriculoperitoneal shunting. Regular shunt reviews are necessary to monitor for dysfunction. Children with severe disabilities should be assessed by a multidisciplinary team for post-TBM care, including pain management and feeding options. Approximately 15% of TBM survivors are partially or completely blind, often due to raised intracranial pressure, optic nerve involvement, or vasculitis. Regular vision assessments and promotion of eye health are recommended. Hypopituitarism, affecting 20% of children post-TBM, may manifest years after recovery and requires early recognition and management. Post-TB lung disease (PTLD) in children and adolescents can result in residual symptoms, such as cough and dyspnea, even after microbiological cure. PTLD increases the risk of recurrent TB, likely due to residual lung damage. End-of-treatment assessments aim to identify children with PTLD, particularly those with severe forms of pulmonary TB or persistent symptoms. Assessment should include symptom screening, clinical examination, nutritional evaluation, and radiological imaging. Lung function testing, including spirometry, should be considered in children aged four years and older with severe PTLD. Bronchodilation may benefit children with obstructive airway disease, but evidence is limited. Referral to a respiratory or pulmonology clinic is recommended for managing bronchiectasis. Pulmonary rehabilitation and airway clearance techniques require further investigation and should be guided by symptoms and recurrent infections. Osteoarticular TB, though uncommon, can have significant long-term consequences in children. It accounts for approximately 1–2% of all pediatric TB cases and 8% of extrapulmonary TB cases.
